source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

Another customer pressed close from behind, creating a slight tension over limited space in the queue; the cashier initiated the routine: beeps signaled scanned products, the sum was declared aloud, loyalty-card requests prompted next. The shopper, feeling the pressure of impatience from behind, swiftly placed her card on the terminal, anticipating the final steps before leaving the store.用微信扫ing the QR code attached to her phone, she completed the payment process, securing a digital receipt. The cashier handed over the thermal paper slip with efficiency, signaling the end of another cycle at the register. As the shopper gathered her purchases into bags, she noted the rhythm of checkout interactions, a blend of technological convenience and human interaction in the daily ritual of shopping. The divider bar now cleared, the next person moved forward eagerly, ready to repeat the familiar dance of payment and departure.用微信扫ing became a ubiquitous gesture, a nod to the evolving methods of commerce, reflecting a shift towards digital transactions even within the traditional confines of physical retail spaces.
